content: Reactive case detection and treatment (RACDT) involves identifying individuals with confirmed malaria cases or those who were likely exposed to the infection at the same time and place as the index case. Only individuals who test positive for malaria are treated with a full therapeutic course of effective antimalarial medication. This approach does not provide population-level prophylaxis, unlike reactive drug administration (RDA). RACDT is typically conducted using point-of-contact rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) but can also involve microscopy or nucleic acid-based tests. RACDT is an active case detection strategy that aims to improve the timeliness and coverage of treatment. It is particularly useful in areas nearing malaria elimination, as it enhances the sensitivity of surveillance systems while maintaining specificity. By focusing on areas with a higher likelihood of malaria transmission, RACDT helps identify additional cases around the index case, which may reveal gaps in the surveillance system. This strategy is essential for countries close to achieving zero indigenous cases, as it provides evidence to support malaria elimination certification. The likely location of infection for the index case is determined through case investigation, which considers the date of symptom onset and the incubation period of the specific parasite species. If the likely location of infection is a residence, RACDT can be conducted within the household of the confirmed case and potentially extended to neighbors, depending on the local epidemiology of malaria. If the index infection was imported, RACDT should target individuals with similar exposure risks, such as co-travelers or co-workers. RACDT is most effective when implemented alongside a strong passive surveillance system that detects suspected cases, tests them parasitologically, and investigates their place of residence. It complements passive surveillance by actively finding cases around index cases. However, the proportion of the population protected from new infections during the post-treatment prophylaxis period is lower with RACDT compared to RDA. Despite this, RACDT may improve treatment adherence, population acceptance, and equity while reducing the risk of unintended consequences and medicine stock depletion. Countries with very low or low malaria transmission but not yet close to elimination should prioritize RDA and reactive indoor residual spraying (IRS) over RACDT. However, RACDT can be added to RDA in countries nearing elimination to strengthen surveillance sensitivity and monitor progress. Post-elimination, RACDT provides additional evidence of a malaria-free status. When RACDT and RDA are implemented together, chemoprevention is provided to everyone, regardless of parasitological test results, while testing results are used to monitor elimination progress. RACDT should be implemented according to standard operating procedures (SOPs). A household listing of all residents within the limits of RDA, as specified by the SOPs, should be developed and verified, along with a list of individuals who may have been co-exposed. The program should aim to test everyone listed, using various approaches to reach all at-risk individuals. Malaria cases detected during RACDT should be treated according to national treatment protocols if chemoprevention through RDA has not already been provided. The evidence on the impact of RACDT on malaria prevalence and incidence is very uncertain, with studies showing low-certainty evidence. Adverse events reported during RACDT were minimal, and the undesirable effects were judged to be trivial. However, the overall certainty of the evidence was judged to be very low, and the balance of effects could not be determined. Community acceptance of RACDT is generally high, with low refusal rates. Challenges include low detection and notification of index cases from private health facilities, complexity in case investigation procedures, and insufficient resources during peak transmission seasons. To address these barriers, programs may benefit from better engagement with the private sector, improved preparation of village clinics, and adequate human resources and diagnostic tools. The cost of RACDT varies depending on program structure and integration into the broader healthcare system. Personnel and community health worker-related costs account for the largest share, while diagnostic tests and medicines contribute less than 10% of total costs. Despite these challenges, RACDT is considered an essential surveillance strategy for countries nearing elimination to ensure no cases remain undetected around confirmed cases.
